stories.title: Where AI is creating jobs for humans — for a while
stories.summary: Data annotation jobs in Karur, India, are growing as humans help improve AI models by analysing video footage for companies mainly in the US. These jobs offer entry-level opportunities for young graduates, paying modest but stable wages, helping address India's youth employment challenges. India aims to develop higher-value AI roles and homegrown AI businesses to ensure long-term economic benefits beyond basic data annotation tasks. KARUR, India – Evidence of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom often looks like the squat, windowless data centres that house acre after acre of hardware. But near the southern tip of India, the city of Karur is teeming with signs of AI’s ascendancy in human form. Hundreds of tech lab workers clog the streets on coffee breaks late on any given weekday afternoon – men and women in their 20s, corporate ID cards dangling from lanyards around their necks. Others work a few hours a weekend from home, supplementing their income by strapping iPhones to their heads and pressing record while they chop vegetables or make the bed. They work in a fast-growing field of AI called data annotation, which – for the moment, at least – requires a human touch. As the sentient backstop for artificial intelligence, data annotators help fix bugs and find blind spots in AI models, improving and refining the programs that steer your car, automate an assembly line and track inventory in retail stores. The work can be rote and less complex than what engineers train for in college, requiring hours in front of a screen to examine video frame by frame. But as AI capabilities change how companies design and produce products – making jobs like coding disappear for college graduates – data annotation is showing how countries like India, with entry-level job shortages and large youth populations, are adapting. Aiswarya Palaniswamy, a 25-year-old with a master’s degree in data analytics, found a job in 2025 with the Karur-based Objectways Technologies, a data-annotation firm whose clients are mainly US companies using AI in their products.
